faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
faq.subtitle: Everything people ask before compiling their first binary

items.question: Does Perry need Node.js or a runtime?
items.answer: Native Perry binaries run without Node.js, Bun, Deno, or an external JavaScript engine installed. They do include the Perry runtime and garbage collector, statically linked. Packages that need engine semantics can use the optional embedded V8 fallback.

items.question: How big are the compiled binaries?
items.answer: Size depends on the target, imports, and build profile. The published examples range from about 330 KB for hello world to about 7 MB for Mango; full-standard-library or optional-V8 builds can be much larger. Treat any size as a measured example, not a universal output size.

items.question: Can I use npm packages?
items.answer: Many pure JavaScript/TypeScript packages compile natively, and roughly 50 package/API implementations are tracked. Compatibility is not universal: packages using native addons, unsupported dynamic behavior, or engine-specific semantics may need the optional V8 fallback or may not work. Run perry check and consult the limitations.

items.question: Which platforms does Perry support?
items.answer: Perry documents 11 targets: macOS, iOS, iPadOS, visionOS, tvOS, watchOS, Android, Wear OS, Windows, Linux, and Web/WASM. Web and WASM are aliases; HarmonyOS is a separate preview. Platform maturity and API coverage differ, so consult the platform guide.

items.question: Is Perry free and open source?
items.answer: The compiler and runtime repository is MIT licensed, and local compilation requires no account. Hosted Perry Publish and commercial support are separate services; availability, limits, and pricing are confirmed in the service or in writing.

items.question: How is Perry different from Bun or Deno compile?
items.answer: Bun and Deno standalone executables bundle their runtimes; Perry native builds compile through LLVM and do not embed a JavaScript engine by default, although they statically link the Perry runtime and GC. Exact size and startup comparisons are version-, platform-, and workload-specific. See the dated <bunLink>Perry vs Bun</bunLink> and <denoLink>Perry vs Deno</denoLink> pages.

items.question: How is Perry different from Electron or Tauri?
items.answer: Electron ships Chromium and Node.js; Tauri uses a system webview with native-side application code. Perry instead maps its UI model to platform widgets where supported. Bundle size and platform capability vary, so use the dated <electronLink>Perry vs Electron</electronLink> and <tauriLink>Perry vs Tauri</tauriLink> comparisons rather than a universal size claim.

items.question: How mature is Perry?
items.answer: Perry is pre-1.0 and changes quickly. Real projects use it today, but language, package, and platform parity are still active work. Review the <showcaseLink>showcase</showcaseLink>, current limitations, and changelog before committing a production workload.

faq.more: More questions? Read the <guideLink>getting-started guide</guideLink> or ask on <discussionsLink>GitHub Discussions</discussionsLink>.

coop.metaTitle: Coop: Native JavaScript/TypeScript hosting for Perry
coop.metaDescription: Coop hosts JavaScript/TypeScript applications compiled by Perry, with shared runtime providers, isolated deployment workers, and content-addressed rollbacks.
coop.tagline: A place for Perry code to rest and run.
coop.intro: Coop turns a directory of Perry-compatible JavaScript/TypeScript into a native application library and serves it over HTTP, while the Perry runtime and standard library are supplied once per machine.
coop.experimental: Experimental infrastructure for code you own
coop.diagramAria: JavaScript/TypeScript is compiled by Perry into an application library, loaded by a Coop worker, and connected to shared runtime providers.
coop.whyTitle: Perry compiles it. Coop keeps it running.
coop.whyBody: The distinction is where the language runtime lives. Coop keeps the application image small and supplies the compatible Perry runtime and standard library at the host level.
coop.perryBody: The application, runtime, garbage collector, and selected standard-library features are linked into one target-specific executable.
coop.coopBody: The application is compiled as an app-only shared library. Compatible runtime providers are built once per machine, and their identity is verified before the app is mapped.
coop.architectureBody: The box, each deployment, and each request have separate responsibilities. Application code never runs in the box daemon.

tiers.title: Daemon · one per machine
tiers.body: Terminates TLS, routes by host and path, owns deployments, artifacts, the admin API, and metrics.

tiers.title: Worker · one per deployment
tiers.body: Loads the application library, owns Perry runtime state, and runs cron and durable queue work.

tiers.title: Invocation · one per request
tiers.body: Runs as a task inside the deployment worker, sharing its address space without spawning a process per request.

coop.workingBody: Coop is tested infrastructure, but it is not yet a finished hosting product. The current implementation includes:
workingItems: JavaScript/TypeScript compilation, HTTP routing, and static mounts
CLI, Prometheus metrics, alerts, and a Grafana dashboard
coop.developerBody: A deployment is a directory with a coop.toml file and one or more handlers. Coop compiles it, caches the result, and starts a local worker.
rightItems: Services and small applications whose code you own
One operator running a portfolio on one machine
Workloads that compile within Perry's JavaScript/TypeScript subset
Teams that value density, explicit artifacts, and fast rollback
coop.notYetTitle: Not a promise Coop makes yet
notYetItems: A sandbox for untrusted third-party code
A Kubernetes replacement or multi-region platform
coop.benchmarkTitle: Density is the thesis. Benchmarks are still the work.
coop.benchmarkBody: Current measurements point in different directions on different workloads. Coop has shown promising density on small Linux applications, while a full Next.js route has cost more CPU than Node.js in another test. Read the methodology before quoting either result.
coop.closingTitle: Build with Perry. Give it a Coop.
coop.closingBody: Explore the source, run the example deployment, and help turn the shared-runtime model into dependable infrastructure.

internals.metaDescription: How Perry selects value representations, specializes known code, uses LLVM, and preserves runtime fallbacks for dynamic JavaScript behavior.
internals.title: Compiler <gradient>Internals</gradient>
internals.subtitle: The key design decisions that make Perry fast
internals.nanBoxing1: Perry uses a 64-bit JavaScript value representation where dynamic values can carry numbers or tagged pointer-like payloads. Representation selection can keep proved values unboxed instead of forcing every value through the generic form.
internals.nanBoxing2: Numbers use IEEE 754 representation where possible; strings, objects, closures, and other heap values use tagged encodings and GC-managed storage. The compiler and runtime cooperate to preserve JavaScript semantics at dynamic boundaries.
internals.monomorphization1: Generics and known call shapes can be specialized at compile time. Perry also preserves dynamic fallbacks where the receiver or value type is not proved.
internals.monomorphization2: Specialization can turn known numeric and object operations into direct machine operations, but TypeScript annotations are mostly erased and do not guarantee a concrete runtime representation by themselves.
internals.staticDispatch1: Known receivers can use direct calls and inlining. Unknown or dynamic receivers use runtime method dispatch, prototype lookup, and class-vtable paths.
internals.staticDispatch2: This hybrid model gives LLVM static optimization opportunities without claiming that every JavaScript method call is resolved at compile time.
internals.zeroCost1: TypeScript types guide compilation, while Perry still links a runtime and garbage collector to implement JavaScript semantics, async work, objects, strings, and dynamic values.
internals.zeroCost2: Interfaces and many annotations erase cleanly, but classes, dynamic dispatch, allocation, and GC can have runtime costs. Perry optimizes proved cases rather than promising zero-cost abstraction universally.

pricing.selfHostTitle: What is open source and self-hostable today?
pricing.selfHostDescription: The Perry compiler and runtime in the linked repository are MIT licensed. That repository includes publish and verification clients plus configurable endpoints, but it does not include a complete public hub, verification service, or worker deployment. Perry therefore does not currently advertise “clone one repo and self-host everything.”
pricing.q1: Does local compilation require an account?
pricing.a1: No. Installing Perry and compiling on your own machine does not require a Perry account.
pricing.q2: What are the hosted quotas and prices?
pricing.a2: They are not promised on this page. Confirm current availability, limits, and charges in the hosted service or in writing before relying on them.
pricing.q3: Can I self-host the complete publish service?
pricing.a3: Not from the Perry compiler repository alone. Custom endpoints are supported by the client, but a complete public hub and worker deployment is not currently included there.

GC, representation selection, dynamic dispatch, startup, binary size, and realistic workload performance.
